title: Curios of the Week #178
author: Ashman, Greg
summary: Greg Ashman's weekly Curios roundup provides pointed commentary on two education controversies. First, his 'Thought burp of the week': Andy Burnham's plan to place vocational training on equal footing with academic subjects from age 14, announced without consulting teachers during school holidays. Ashman dismantles the policy not because vocational education is bad, but because its practical implementation in schools consistently fails for structural reasons — lathes, industrial kitchens, and workshops are expensive and constrained, so courses become ersatz academic exercises that everyone recognises as shams. Second, the 'Trolling of the week': Ashman's endorsement of Stephen Vainker's argument that the Arday case reflects a broader institutional failure in educational academia — the detachment from classroom realities, derivative unoriginal scholarship, and the use of identity markers in hiring over quality. Together the two sections constitute a sharp weekly brief on education's most contested fault lines.
points: There is a view that part of the issue is the UK's class system — vocational education is seen as lesser than academic subjects. That may be a factor, but it's not the main one.

The issues with vocational training at 14 are practical ones — lathes, copper pipes, industrial kitchens, model farms are expensive, and where schools can afford them they become a highly constrained resource.

Middle class teachers tasked with running vocational courses then make them look much like the rest of school — students spend time with pen and paper writing business cases and marketing campaigns. Everyone knows it is a sham.

Vainker argues that educational academia has produced too much work becoming detached from the realities and requirements of classroom practice; where there are implications, they are generally facile.
Secondary characteristics, including but not limited to identity markers, play a central role in hiring and promotion over and above ability and quality — I think there is something to this.
quotes: Unfortunately, I did not fully appreciate that Vainker had given his post a highly provocative title: “Leave Jason Arday alone - this is a scandal of academic educational leadership.” I believe that if the allegations are proven, Arday should face consequences.

Nevertheless, when I posted the following on Twitter/X, the replies came mainly from people assuming that I was a supporter of Arday: Again, I am not commenting on the substance of any allegations against Arday, Hattie, BERA or anyone else.

Trolling of the week My ability to blithely wade into emotive arguments was in evidence this week when I stumbled into the Jason Arday controversy and accidentally trolled a large number of angry, possibly racist, people on Twitter/X.

I also think that misguided attempts by governments to send more and more young people to university has resulted in many taking on substantial debt to complete courses that will never be a return on that investment.

Back in the 2000s, my local Labour MP explained to me that it did not matter if some of these degrees were hollow, it would make the bearers middle class and so their children, in turn, would have better outcomes.
Vainker takes aim at other figures, such as John Hattie and editors at the British Educational Research Association (BERA) and clearly wants to see action taken on these fronts.
If proven, plagiarism is a serious professional failing, but I have always been more interested in whether academics are right or wrong than their personal integrity.
